topics.summary: Stanford researchers measured 'sycophancy' (excessive agreement and flattery) in 11 state-of-the-art large language models, comparing their advice to human judgments, including Reddit's Am I The Asshole community, on interpersonal conflicts, deception and harmful actions. The models affirmed users' actions about 49% more often than humans did. Three preregistered experiments with 2,405 people then had participants discuss real or hypothetical conflicts with flattering or neutral AI. One sycophantic conversation made people more convinced they were right and less willing to apologize or repair the relationship, yet they trusted the flattering model more and preferred to use it again, an incentive problem for AI companies optimizing engagement. Topics: AI alignment and safety, human-computer interaction, social psychology, moral judgment, conflict resolution, chatbot design and accountability.

Scenarios covered everyday conflicts, deception and harmful or illegal acts

topics.summary: Google's Co-Scientist is a multi-agent AI system built on Gemini that generates, debates and refines scientific hypotheses. Agents propose ideas, critique them, and rank them in an Elo-style tournament; spending more compute at test time keeps improving hypothesis quality. It was validated in biomedicine: it proposed drugs to repurpose for acute myeloid leukaemia that worked in cell experiments, suggested new treatment targets for liver fibrosis, and independently re-derived an unpublished explanation from Imperial College for how phage-inducible chromosomal islands, bacterial gene parasites, hijack diverse phage tails to spread across species, relevant to antimicrobial resistance. Topics: AI for science, large language models, agents, drug discovery, cancer, microbiology, bacteriophages, automating research.

topics.summary: A Cornell-led Nature Sustainability analysis projected the environmental footprint of AI servers in the United States from 2024 to 2030. Depending on growth, AI servers could use 731 to 1,125 million cubic meters of water a year and add 24 to 44 million tonnes of CO2-equivalent annually. The industry is unlikely to meet net-zero pledges by 2030 without relying on uncertain carbon offsets and water restoration. Best practices could cut emissions by up to 73% and water by 86%, mainly by siting servers in central states such as Texas, Montana, Nebraska and South Dakota with abundant wind and solar and low water stress, though Texas might need more new power than its current renewable output. Topics: data centers, energy systems, water footprint, climate policy, electricity grids, renewable energy, sustainability of computing.

topics.summary: ETH Zurich engineers built a clinically oriented magnetic microrobot for targeted drug delivery: a dissolvable gelatin capsule about 1.7 mm across, loaded with iron oxide nanoparticles for magnetic steering, a contrast agent so it shows up on X-ray fluoroscopy, and a drug such as the clot-dissolving enzyme tPA used for stroke. A clinical electromagnetic navigation system and a custom release catheter steered it through realistic models of human blood vessels and through cranial arteries in pigs and sheep, where it was tracked live and released its cargo on target. The goal is to deliver drugs locally instead of flooding the whole body. Topics: medical robotics, magnetism, biomedical engineering, stroke treatment, interventional radiology, drug delivery, nanoparticles.

topics.summary: The Global Carbon Budget team (Friedlingstein, Le Quere and colleagues) reconciled estimates of where humanity's CO2 goes. Atmospheric CO2 reached 423 ppm in 2024 and human-caused warming 1.36 C. Revised accounting shows the natural land sink is substantially smaller than previously estimated, emissions from land-use change are larger, and the ocean sink is about 15% larger than the land sink. Climate change itself has weakened the sinks, especially on land, adding 8.3 ppm to atmospheric CO2 since 1960. Combined with deforestation, it has turned Southeast Asian and much of South American tropical forest from carbon sinks into sources. Topics: climate science, carbon cycle, oceanography, forests, deforestation, Earth system models, Paris Agreement, climate policy.

facts: A net absorber, or carbon 'sink', takes in more CO2 than it releases
Heat and drought slow tree growth and kill trees, which then release carbon
Cutting forests releases their stored carbon and ends future absorption

Weakened sinks have added 8.3 parts per million of CO2 since 1960

topics.summary: Cornell and Berkeley researchers analyzed 2.1 million preprints, 28,000 peer review reports and 246 million online accesses to see how large language models are changing science. Scientists who adopted LLMs to draft manuscripts increased their output by 23.7% to 89.3% depending on field and author background, with large gains for non-native English speakers. Before LLMs, more complex writing went with higher-quality papers; with LLM use the relationship reversed, producing polished-sounding but substantively weaker manuscripts. LLM adopters also read and cite more diverse prior work, including books and younger, less-cited papers. The authors argue journals, funders and tenure committees must rethink how they judge research. Topics: science of science, academic publishing, peer review, ChatGPT, research productivity, bibliometrics.

topics.summary: Cambridge neuroscientists pooled diffusion MRI scans from 4,216 people aged 0 to 90 and tracked 12 graph-theory measures of how the brain's white-matter network is organized. Projecting these onto low-dimensional manifolds revealed four major topological turning points, around ages 9, 32, 66 and 83, splitting life into five epochs. From childhood to about 32 the network keeps becoming more efficiently integrated, an extended adolescence-like phase; adulthood is the longest stable epoch; after about 66 the network becomes more segregated; after 83 the age relationship weakens. Turning points may align with puberty, life milestones and risks for mental health and dementia. Topics: brain development, aging, neuroimaging, connectomics, network science, cognitive neuroscience, lifespan psychology.

topics.summary: Stanford researchers built SleepFM, a foundation model trained on more than 585,000 hours of polysomnography, overnight sleep-lab recordings of brain waves, heart activity, breathing and muscle signals, from about 65,000 people. Using contrastive learning, it turns a single night into an embedding that predicts 130 future diseases with a C-index of at least 0.75, including death (0.84), dementia (0.85), heart failure (0.80), chronic kidney disease and stroke, and it generalized to an unseen cohort, the Sleep Heart Health Study. It also performs standard sleep staging and apnea detection. Topics: sleep medicine, machine learning in medicine, foundation models, wearables, dementia, cardiology, risk prediction.

Accuracy for dementia: 0.85 (0.5 = coin flip, 1 = perfect)
It worked on a separate group of people it had never seen

topics.summary: A Swedish nationwide study paired grasslands with neighboring managed forests to follow what happens to soil microbes when farmland is abandoned and turns back into forest, the largest land-use change in the Global North. Microbes changed through thresholds rather than gradually: taxonomic diversity fell while functional diversity rose, and nutrient-cycling genes for carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus became more specialized with less redundancy, a trade-off between diversity of functions and backup. Fungal functional diversity drove higher carbon-processing capacity, and leaf litter quality linked plant and microbe communities. Rewilding is not automatically a win for soil biodiversity and carbon. Topics: soil ecology, microbiology, fungi, land abandonment, rewilding, forestry, carbon storage, ecosystem succession.

truth.text: When abandoned farmland turns back into forest, its soil ends up with fewer kinds of microbes but a wider range of jobs they can do, with fungi leading the change.
facts: Soil microbes are bacteria and fungi that break down dead plants
'Jobs' means chemistry like recycling carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus
The study paired Swedish grasslands with neighboring forests nationwide
Changes came in sudden jumps, not gradually
Farm abandonment is the biggest land-use change in Europe and North America

topics.summary: Researchers from Heidelberg, Harvard and partners used a health-augmented macroeconomic model across 204 countries to estimate diabetes's economic cost from 2020 to 2050, counting lost labor from deaths and illness, diverted treatment spending and informal caregiving. Without informal care the burden is 10.2 trillion international dollars, about 0.22% of global GDP every year; including unpaid family care it rises to 78.8 trillion (1.72% of GDP), more than six times larger. Absolute costs are highest in the US, China and India; per-person and relative burdens are highest in places like American Samoa and Australia, while much of Africa and South Asia show lower relative burden. More than one in ten adults has diabetes. Topics: health economics, global health, diabetes, caregiving, GDP, public policy.

Without family care: $10.2 trillion, 0.22% of world GDP yearly
With it: 1.72% of world GDP every year
Biggest totals: US, China and India; the model covered 204 countries

topics.summary: Oxford researchers modeled 24 maritime chokepoints, narrow passages like the Suez Canal, Panama Canal, Strait of Hormuz, Malacca Strait and Taiwan Strait, and eight hazards: cyclones, drought, earthquakes, terrorism, armed and interstate conflict, blockages and piracy. About 192 billion US dollars of trade a year is expected to be disrupted, mostly from geopolitical risk at the Taiwan Strait and Suez Canal and combined hazards at Bab el-Mandeb near Yemen. Expected economic losses are 10.7 billion dollars a year plus 3.4 billion from higher freight costs. Exposed countries include neighbors of these straits but also distant ones in West Africa and Central Asia; Russia, Kazakhstan and Tajikistan depend on six chokepoints each. Topics: shipping, global trade, supply chains, geopolitics, risk analysis, Red Sea Houthi attacks, Panama Canal drought.

topics.summary: SURPASS-CVOT, a double-blind NEJM trial, randomized 13,299 people with type 2 diabetes and atherosclerotic heart disease to weekly tirzepatide (Mounjaro, a dual GLP-1 and GIP agonist known for large weight loss) or dulaglutide (Trulicity, a GLP-1 drug already proven to reduce heart events). Over a median of four years, tirzepatide was noninferior for the composite of cardiovascular death, heart attack or stroke (801 vs 862 events, hazard ratio 0.92, confidence interval 0.83 to 1.01), so not statistically superior. Gastrointestinal side effects were more common with tirzepatide. Topics: cardiology, diabetes, obesity drugs, GLP-1, clinical trials, pharmacology.

topics.summary: Sakana AI, Oxford and UBC researchers present The AI Scientist, a pipeline using foundation models in an agentic system to automate the whole research cycle in machine learning: generating ideas, searching literature, writing code, running experiments, plotting, writing the manuscript and reviewing it with an automated reviewer. In a template mode and an open-ended agentic-search mode it produced diverse papers. Three AI-written manuscripts were submitted, with organizers' consent, to a workshop at a top machine-learning conference (ICLR) whose reviewers knew some submissions were AI-generated but not which; one scored 6, 7 and 6, above the acceptance threshold of a workshop with a 70% acceptance rate. Topics: AI research automation, LLM agents, peer review, scientific integrity, machine learning.

topics.summary: JWST revealed 'little red dots', compact red galaxies in the early universe with broad hydrogen and helium emission lines, debated as either supermassive black holes or intense starbursts, with odd traits such as black holes too massive for their hosts and very weak X-ray and radio emission. Analyzing the best spectra, the authors show the lines are broadened by electron scattering around a narrow core, requiring dense, compact ionized gas only light-days across, which with their luminosity can only be explained by black hole accretion. The narrow cores imply masses of 100,000 to 10 million suns, about 100 times lower than earlier estimates: young black holes growing near the Eddington limit inside a dense gas cocoon that also hides X-rays and radio. Topics: astronomy, black holes, galaxy formation, cosmology, JWST, spectroscopy.

truth.text: The mysterious 'little red dots' spotted by the James Webb telescope are most likely young black holes wrapped in thick cocoons of gas, far lighter than first thought.
facts: The James Webb Space Telescope sees the early universe in infrared light

'Far lighter': 100,000 to 10 million suns, about 100 times less than estimated
The thick gas cocoon also explains why they give off almost no X-rays

topics.summary: The glymphatic system is the brain's waste-clearance network, in which cerebrospinal fluid flushes the tissue, mostly during sleep. In a multi-site randomized crossover trial, 39 healthy older adults spent one night sleeping normally and one night sleep-deprived in a lab, wearing a new device that measured sleep EEG, cerebrovascular compliance (pulse transit time) and brain-tissue resistance to fluid flow by impedance spectroscopy. Lower tissue resistance, more compliant vessels, higher heart-rate variability and more deep slow-wave sleep predicted bigger overnight rises of Alzheimer's markers amyloid beta and tau in morning blood, evidence that sleep-driven glymphatic flow clears these proteins from brain to plasma in humans. Topics: sleep, Alzheimer's disease, neuroscience, aging, biomarkers, clinical trials, medical devices.

truth.text: A sleep-lab trial in older adults found that deep sleep helps the brain flush Alzheimer's-linked proteins out into the blood, direct evidence of the brain's nightly 'rinse' in humans.
facts: The 'rinse' is the glymphatic system: spinal fluid washing through brain tissue
The proteins are amyloid and tau, which build up in Alzheimer's
39 people slept normally one night and stayed awake another
More deep sleep predicted more of both proteins in morning blood tests

topics.summary: The Psychiatric Genomics Consortium combined genetic association data for 14 childhood- and adult-onset psychiatric disorders covering 1,056,201 cases. Genomic structural equation modeling found five underlying genetic factors explaining about two thirds of each disorder's genetic variance: schizophrenia and bipolar disorder; internalizing (major depression, PTSD, anxiety); neurodevelopmental (ADHD, autism, Tourette's); compulsive (OCD, anorexia); and substance use. The factors linked to 238 pleiotropic loci; schizophrenia-bipolar and internalizing disorders shared most of their signal with very few disorder-specific loci. Shared genes pointed to broad processes like transcriptional regulation. Results challenge current diagnostic boundaries such as the DSM. Topics: psychiatry, genetics, genomics, mental health, schizophrenia, depression, autism.

truth.text: A genetic study of over a million psychiatric patients found that 14 disorders fall into five genetic clusters, with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder sharing most of their genetic risk.
facts: Pooled DNA data on 1,056,201 patients with psychiatric diagnoses
Clusters: psychotic, depression-anxiety, neurodevelopmental, compulsive, substance use
For example, autism and ADHD cluster together, as do OCD and anorexia

topics.summary: On January 14, 2025, LIGO recorded GW250114, the loudest gravitational wave so far (network signal-to-noise ratio 76), from two merging black holes; Virgo and KAGRA were offline. Like a struck bell, the remnant black hole rings down with quasinormal modes whose frequencies general relativity fixes by mass and spin alone (the Kerr metric). The data require at least two modes, the fundamental tone and its first overtone, matching Kerr to tens of percent, and bound the main frequency within a few percent of the prediction. Inspiral, merger and ringdown tests were as strong or up to three times stronger than combining dozens of earlier events: the most stringent single-event confirmation of general relativity. Topics: physics, gravitational waves, black holes, Einstein, relativity, astrophysics.

truth.text: The loudest gravitational wave ever recorded let physicists 'hear' a newborn black hole vibrate like a struck bell at two distinct pitches, exactly as Einstein's theory predicts.
facts: Gravitational waves are ripples in space itself, made by colliding heavy objects
After two black holes merge, the new one shakes and settles, emitting set 'pitches'
Einstein's relativity says those pitches depend only on the black hole's mass and spin
Recorded by LIGO on January 14, 2025; the clearest such signal so far
This one event tested relativity better than dozens of earlier detections combined

topics.summary: Oxford researchers ran a randomized, preregistered study with 1,298 UK adults given ten medical scenarios written by doctors, asked to identify likely conditions and the right action, from self-care to calling an ambulance. Participants used GPT-4o, Llama 3 or Command R+, or any source they liked (control). Alone, the models named relevant conditions 94.9% of the time and the right disposition 56.3%. With the same models, people found relevant conditions under 34.5% of the time and the right action under 44.2%, no better than controls. Failures came from people giving incomplete information and from models offering several options (2.21 on average) that users chose poorly among. Medical exam benchmarks and simulated patients did not predict these failures. Topics: AI in medicine, chatbots, human-computer interaction, patient safety, health informatics.

truth.text: Chatbots alone diagnosed medical scenarios correctly 95% of the time, but ordinary people using the same chatbots got it right less than 35% of the time, no better than without them.

topics.summary: Google DeepMind and Cambridge researchers developed a psychometric framework to give validated personality tests, the IPIP-NEO Big Five and others, to 18 large language models across thousands of prompt variations, and to check reliability and construct validity as psychologists do for humans. Larger and instruction-tuned models gave reliable, valid personality measurements; base and small models did not. Prompts could shape personality along chosen dimensions, such as more extraverted or less neurotic, and the shaped traits carried into downstream text such as social media posts. The authors discuss risks such as persuasive or manipulative personas and benefits for responsible AI. Topics: psychology, psychometrics, personality, large language models, AI safety, chatbots.

topics.summary: Researchers ran a process-based crop model inside an Earth system model to project how drought affects global food security by 2050 for maize, soybean, rice and wheat. Global drought losses are projected to be under 2%, but 62 countries may lose more than 10% and 24 countries more than 20% of production. Vulnerability is highest in countries with lower GDP and fast population growth, often in Africa and South Asia, so global averages hide severe local food insecurity. Topics: agriculture, climate change, drought, food security, crop modeling, development economics.
